records.topic: The 26-Kilometre Strait Guarding the Red Sea
records.coreQuestion: Why can a strait just 26 kilometres wide reroute a share of the world's oil?
records.openingLine: Why 9% of seaborne oil needs one strait.
records.secondBeat: Bab el-Mandeb is just 26 kilometres wide at its narrowest.
records.dependency: Tankers and container ships between the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea and Suez depend on passage through Bab el-Mandeb.
records.mechanism: Traffic is confined to two narrow inbound and outbound lanes through a strait 26 km wide at its narrowest.
records.bottleneck: There is no alternative sea route into the Red Sea from the south.
records.failureConsequence: A closure forces ships around the Cape of Good Hope, adding time, fuel and insurance cost.
records.resilience: Pipelines and rerouting around Africa absorb part of the flow at higher cost.
records.expectedConsequence: freight and insurance costs rise first as ships divert
visualScenes: two tanker lanes through the strait
Red Sea to Suez route line
Cape of Good Hope diversion map
editorialTitles: The Narrow Strait at the Red Sea's Gate
Why Bab el-Mandeb Can Reroute World Trade

facts.claim: The Bab al-Mandab Strait is 26 kilometres (14 nautical miles) wide at its narrowest point, limiting tanker traffic to two 2-mile-wide channels for inbound and outbound shipments.
In 2006, an estimated 3.3 million barrels of oil passed through the strait per day, out of a world total of about 43 million barrels per day moved by tankers.
In 2017, total petroleum flows through the Bab al-Mandab Strait accounted for about 9% of total seaborne-traded petroleum.
In April 2026, Houthi official Hussein al-Ezzi warned that the Bab al-Mandab strait could be closed.

narration.text: Why 9% of seaborne oil needs one strait.
Bab el-Mandeb is just 26 kilometres wide at its narrowest.
Tankers use two lanes, each about 2 miles wide.
It links the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and Suez.
Back in 2006, about 3.3 million barrels a day passed through.
Close it, and ships must detour around Africa.
That's why a gap this narrow can reprice global freight.

records.coreQuestion: Why does a whole sea's shipping depend on a channel 700 metres wide inside a city?
records.openingLine: Why Black Sea trade narrows to 700 metres.
records.secondBeat: That's the Bosporus at its tightest, inside Istanbul.
records.dependency: Black Sea exports of grain, oil and metals depend on transit through the Bosporus.
records.mechanism: Ships follow a winding 31 km channel through Istanbul, with long vessels pre-booking passage.
records.bottleneck: At its narrowest the strait is only 700 m wide, with sharp turns and heavy local ferry traffic.
records.failureConsequence: A grounding or collision can halt transits and queue ships at both ends.
records.resilience: Pipelines and rail carry part of the cargo, but most bulk trade has no other sea exit.
records.expectedConsequence: queues form at both ends of the strait within hours
visualScenes: satellite map of the Bosporus through Istanbul
ship queue at the strait entrance
editorialTitles: The City Strait That Controls a Sea
Why the Bosporus Is a Global Chokepoint

facts.claim: The strait is 31 km (17 nmi) long, with a width of 3,329 m at the northern entrance and 2,826 m at the southern entrance.
Its maximum width is 3,420 m between Umuryeri and Büyükdere Limanı, and minimum width is 700 m between Kandilli Point and Aşiyan.
The depth of the Bosporus varies from 13 to 110 m (43 to 361 ft) in midstream with an average of 65 m (213 ft).
Ships over 150 metres long or 10 metres deep must pre-book their passage.
In 2022 the dues levied by Turkey for freight ships increased 500% to US$4 per ton, the first change since 1983.
The city of Istanbul's metropolitan population of 17 million inhabitants extends inland from both banks.

narration.text: Why Black Sea trade narrows to 700 metres.
That's the Bosporus at its tightest, inside Istanbul.
The strait runs 31 kilometres through a city of 17 million.
Its depth ranges from 13 to 110 metres midstream.
Ships over 150 metres long must pre-book their passage.
In 2022, Turkey raised transit dues 500%, the first change since 1983.
One stalled tanker here can back up a whole sea's exports.
That's why a city channel controls a sea's access to the world.

records.topic: The 57-Kilometre Tunnel Carrying Freight Under the Alps
records.coreQuestion: What happens to Europe's north–south freight when one flat tunnel under the Alps shuts?
records.openingLine: One derailment shut the Gotthard for a year.
records.secondBeat: The tunnel runs 57 kilometres beneath the Alps.
records.dependency: Freight between northern Europe and Italy relies on the flat Gotthard Base Tunnel route.
records.mechanism: A 57 km low-level tunnel lets heavy freight trains cross the Alps without steep mountain grades.
records.bottleneck: Two single-track tubes and crossover stations concentrate capacity in one structure.
records.failureConsequence: A derailment in 2023 damaged the tunnel and closed one tube for over a year.
records.resilience: The older mountain line and other Alpine corridors absorb traffic at lower capacity.
records.expectedConsequence: trains divert to slower, steeper routes and capacity drops
visualScenes: cross-section of the Alps with the tunnel
freight train in a tunnel tube
editorialTitles: The Tunnel That Flattened the Alps
What One Derailment Did to Alpine Freight

facts.claim: With a route length of 57.09 km (35.47 mi), it is the world's longest railway and deepest traffic tunnel and the first flat, low-level route through the Alps.
It is the deepest railway tunnel in the world, with a maximum depth of 2,450 m (8,040 ft).
Since the GBT is in full service, standard freight trains of up to 3,600 t are able to pass this natural barrier.
Completed in 2016, the final cost was reported to be CHF 12.2 billion (US$12 billion).
A freight train derailment in August 2023 forced the tunnel's closure for over a year before reopening in September 2024.
The derailed wagon pulled more than 20 following wagons off the tracks.
Freight trains were allowed to use the east tunnel from 23 August whilst passenger services remained rerouted.

narration.text: One derailment shut the Gotthard for a year.
The tunnel runs 57 kilometres beneath the Alps.
It's the world's longest railway tunnel, up to 2,450 metres deep.
Its flat route lets 3,600-tonne freight trains cross the mountains.
It cost 12.2 billion Swiss francs and opened in 2016.
In 2023, one derailed wagon pulled over 20 more off the tracks.
Freight squeezed into one tube while passenger trains detoured.
That's why one flat tunnel carries so much of Europe's freight.

records.coreQuestion: Why does one Dutch port matter to a hinterland of 500 million people?
records.openingLine: One port serves a hinterland of 500 million.
records.secondBeat: Rotterdam's port stretches 40 kilometres to the sea.
records.dependency: Industries and consumers across Europe depend on cargo moving through Rotterdam into rivers, rail and pipelines.
records.mechanism: A 40 km chain of port areas links deep-sea shipping to inland barges, rail and road.
records.bottleneck: Much of Europe's inland distribution is organised around this single gateway.
records.failureConsequence: Disruption delays supplies to factories and shops far inland.
records.resilience: Antwerp, Hamburg and other North Sea ports can absorb some diverted cargo.
records.expectedConsequence: inland deliveries slip as cargo waits for another gateway
visualScenes: aerial map of Rotterdam port areas
editorialTitles: The Port Behind Europe's Supply Chains
Why Rotterdam Matters More Than Its Ranking

facts.claim: From 1962 until 2004, it was the world's busiest port by annual cargo tonnage.
In 2020, Rotterdam was the world's tenth-largest container port in terms of twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU) handled.
Covering 105 square kilometres (41 sq mi), the port of Rotterdam stretches over a distance of 40 kilometres (25 mi).
Rotterdam consists of five distinct port areas and three distribution parks that facilitate the needs of a hinterland with over 500 million consumers throughout the continent of Europe.

narration.text: One port serves a hinterland of 500 million.
Rotterdam's port stretches 40 kilometres to the sea.
It covers 105 square kilometres of docks and terminals.
From 1962 to 2004, it was the world's busiest port.
In 2020, it ranked tenth for containers.
Its value is the reach inland, into Europe's river and rail network.
A disruption here ripples through factories hundreds of kilometres away.
That's why Rotterdam matters more than its ranking suggests.

records.topic: The Port Where 90% of Boxes Just Switch Ships
records.coreQuestion: What happens when the port where most boxes only change ships slows down?
records.openingLine: Why 90% of Singapore's boxes just switch ships.
records.secondBeat: Singapore is less a destination than a switchyard.
records.dependency: Shipping lines connecting Asia, Europe and Oceania rely on Singapore to swap containers between services.
records.mechanism: Containers arrive on one vessel and leave on another, feeding dozens of regional routes.
records.bottleneck: Transshipment concentrates connections: a delay in one hub spreads to every linked route.
records.failureConsequence: Congestion strands containers bound for many other ports, not just Singapore.
records.resilience: Nearby hubs such as Port Klang and Tanjung Pelepas can absorb some transfers.
records.expectedConsequence: missed connections ripple across regional shipping schedules
visualScenes: container crane swapping boxes between ships
editorialTitles: The Port That's Mostly a Switchyard
Why Singapore's Delays Travel So Far

facts.claim: Around 90% of its container throughput was transshipment traffic in 2024.
Marine fuel sales also reached 56.77 million tons, up 3.4% from the previous year.
Operations at the Tuas mega port began in September 2021, and officially opened on 1 September 2022, with three berths fully operational.
Eight more berths commenced service by February 2025.
It was ranked as the world's busiest port in terms of total cargo tonnage handled until 2010, when it was surpassed by the Port of Shanghai.

narration.text: Why 90% of Singapore's boxes just switch ships.
Singapore is less a destination than a switchyard.
In 2024, around 90% of its container traffic was transshipment.
It also sold 56.77 million tons of marine fuel.
Its new Tuas mega port opened in 2022 with 3 berths.
8 more berths entered service by February 2025.
If Singapore stalls, cargo for dozens of ports waits offshore.
That's why a city-state's port sets the pace for Asian shipping.

records.coreQuestion: Why does nuclear power depend on a machine that only a few countries can build?
records.openingLine: Nuclear fuel depends on tubes spinning 50,000 rpm.
records.secondBeat: Gas centrifuges separate uranium-235 from uranium-238.
records.dependency: Most nuclear reactors need fuel enriched in uranium-235 by gas centrifuges.
records.mechanism: Uranium hexafluoride gas spins at high speed; slightly lighter U-235 molecules concentrate toward the centre.
records.bottleneck: Each machine enriches only slightly, so fuel needs long cascades of precision centrifuges.
records.failureConsequence: Loss of enrichment capacity leaves reactors without new fuel loads.
records.resilience: Stockpiles and a few international suppliers buffer shortages for a time.
records.expectedConsequence: fuel lead times stretch as enrichment capacity tightens
editorialTitles: The Spinning Machine Behind Nuclear Fuel
Why So Few Countries Can Enrich Uranium

facts.claim: A prominent use of gas centrifuges is for the separation of uranium-235 (235U) from uranium-238 (238U).
Centrifuges are ramped up to the required speed, generally in excess of 50,000 rpm.
The early units were typically around 2 metres long; the present generation are over 4 metres in length.
This process yields higher concentrations of 235U while using significantly less energy compared to the gaseous diffusion process.
The stream that is slightly enriched in 235U is withdrawn and fed into the next higher stage, while the slightly depleted stream is recycled back into the next lower stage.

narration.text: Nuclear fuel depends on tubes spinning 50,000 rpm.
Gas centrifuges separate uranium-235 from uranium-238.
Heavier molecules drift outward. Slightly lighter ones collect inward.
Each stage enriches only slightly, so machines are chained in cascades.
Modern units are over 4 metres long.
They replaced gaseous diffusion, using far less energy.
Few countries can build them, and the know-how is tightly controlled.
That's why nuclear power runs on a machine few can make.

records.topic: Why America's Emergency Oil Drains So Slowly
records.coreQuestion: Why can't America's emergency oil reserve replace imports, even when it's full?
records.openingLine: Why 285.4 million barrels can't flow fast.
records.secondBeat: Its maximum withdrawal is 2.7 million barrels a day.
records.dependency: U.S. energy security in a supply shock depends on oil stored in underground caverns in Louisiana and Texas.
records.mechanism: Oil is pumped out of underground storage at a maximum combined rate of 2.7 million barrels a day.
records.bottleneck: The withdrawal rate, not the stockpile size, limits how much the reserve can cover.
records.failureConsequence: In a large disruption, the reserve covers only part of daily demand and runs down over months.
records.resilience: Commercial inventories and international stock releases add to the buffer.
records.expectedConsequence: the reserve slows a price spike but cannot fully replace lost supply
visualScenes: map of reserve sites in Louisiana and Texas
editorialTitles: The Emergency Oil That Can't Flow Fast
Why the Petroleum Reserve Buys Time, Not Supply

facts.claim: Its underground tanks in Louisiana and Texas have capacity for 714 million barrels (113,500,000 m3).
As of September 4, 2026, the inventory was 285.4 million barrels (45,370,000 m3).
This equates to about 14 days' worth of oil at 2026 daily U.S. consumption levels of 20.1 million barrels per day.
The maximum total withdrawal capability from the SPR is only 2.7 million barrels per day, so it would take about 106 days to use the entire inventory.

narration.text: Why 285.4 million barrels can't flow fast.
Its maximum withdrawal is 2.7 million barrels a day.
Underground caverns in Louisiana and Texas hold up to 714 million barrels.
That was the stock in September 2026.
That's about 14 days of American consumption.
But draining it fully would take about 106 days.
So the reserve buys time. It can't replace imports.
That's why the pump rate matters as much as the stockpile.

records.topic: The Radio Beams That Land Planes in Fog
records.coreQuestion: How do planes land when pilots can't see the runway?
records.openingLine: Why fog landings depend on 2 radio beams.
records.secondBeat: One steers left-right. The other sets the descent.
records.dependency: Low-visibility landings at major airports depend on the instrument landing system's radio beams.
records.mechanism: A localizer gives horizontal guidance and a glideslope gives vertical guidance down to the runway.
records.bottleneck: Precision approaches need calibrated transmitters that shut down quickly on any fault.
records.failureConsequence: Without ILS in fog, flights divert or hold, cutting airport capacity.
records.resilience: Satellite-based LPV approaches now cover many airports as a backup.
records.expectedConsequence: arrivals divert or hold when visibility drops
visualScenes: CAT I versus CAT III minimums chart
editorialTitles: How Planes Land When Pilots Can't See
The Radio Beams Behind Fog Landings

facts.claim: ILS uses two directional radio signals, the localizer (108 to 112 MHz frequency), which provides horizontal guidance, and the glideslope (329.15 to 335 MHz frequency) for vertical guidance.
A CAT I localizer must shut down within 10 seconds of detecting a fault, but a CAT III localizer must shut down in less than 2 seconds.
After the formation of ICAO in 1947, ILS was selected as the first international standard precision approach system and was published in ICAO Annex 10 in 1950.
By 2015, the number of US airports supporting ILS-like LPV approaches exceeded the number of ILS installations.

narration.text: Why fog landings depend on 2 radio beams.
One steers left-right. The other sets the descent.
The localizer transmits between 108 and 112 megahertz.
The glideslope uses 329.15 to 335 megahertz.
A CAT III localizer must shut down within 2 seconds of a fault.
A wrong beam is worse than no beam at all.
ICAO made ILS the first international precision approach standard.
That's why decades-old radio still guides the final approach.

records.topic: The Radio Signal Every Big Ship Must Broadcast
records.coreQuestion: How do thousands of ships share one radio channel to announce where they are?
records.openingLine: Why ships share 2,250 radio slots every minute.
records.secondBeat: That's how AIS packs thousands of position reports together.
records.dependency: Collision avoidance, vessel traffic services and port planning depend on AIS position reports.
records.mechanism: Transponders broadcast position reports in shared time slots on VHF frequencies.
records.bottleneck: Coastal reception is limited to VHF range; open-ocean coverage relies on satellites.
records.failureConsequence: When a transponder is switched off, the ship disappears from shared traffic pictures.
records.resilience: Radar, satellite imagery and patrols can partly fill gaps.
records.expectedConsequence: dark ships create blind spots for traffic control and safety
visualScenes: ship icons on a live traffic map
VHF antenna on a ship mast
time-slot diagram on a radio frequency
satellite picking up signals over ocean
editorialTitles: The Radio Signal That Maps Every Big Ship
Why a Ship Can Vanish With One Switch

facts.claim: Recent regulations have mandated the installation of AIS systems on all Safety Of Life At Sea (SOLAS) vessels and vessels over 300 tons.
This was the first mandate for the use of AIS equipment and affected approximately 100,000 vessels.
A position report from one station fits into one of 2,250 time slots established every 60 seconds on each frequency.
Shore reception is limited to the VHF range, about 10–20 nautical miles.
In late 2011 and early 2012, ORBCOMM and Luxspace launched the Vesselsat AIS microsatellites.

narration.text: Why ships share 2,250 radio slots every minute.
That's how AIS packs thousands of position reports together.
It's mandatory on SOLAS vessels and ships over 300 tons.
The first mandate covered about 100,000 vessels.
Ground stations hear it only 10 to 20 nautical miles out.
Satellites now pick it up across open oceans.
Switch it off, and a ship vanishes from traffic pictures.
That's why sea traffic depends on ships announcing themselves.

records.topic: The Train Safety System That Arrived 5 Years Late
records.coreQuestion: Why did a train-stopping safety system take twelve years to install across U.S. railroads?
records.openingLine: America's train safety system arrived 5 years late.
records.secondBeat: Congress set a 2015 deadline. It finished in 2020.
records.dependency: Passenger and freight trains on required U.S. routes depend on positive train control to prevent certain crashes.
records.mechanism: Onboard, wayside and office systems share data so the train can be stopped automatically before an overspeed or signal violation.
records.bottleneck: Every railroad sharing the same tracks had to install interoperable equipment.
records.failureConsequence: Where PTC is missing or fails, safety falls back on crews alone.
records.resilience: Signals and operating rules remain as the base safety layer.
records.expectedConsequence: trains run slower or under restrictions when PTC is unavailable
editorialTitles: The Safety System U.S. Railroads Couldn't Rush
Why Positive Train Control Took 12 Years

facts.claim: In September 2008, Congress considered a new law that set a deadline of December 15, 2015 for implementation of PTC technology across most of the US rail network.
As of June 2015, only seven commuter systems (29 percent of those represented by APTA) were expecting to make the deadline.
In October 2015, Congress passed a bill extending the compliance deadline by three years, to December 31, 2018.
Only four railroads met the December 2018 deadline; the other 37 got extensions to December 2020.
PTC was installed and operational on 100% of the statutory-required trackage by December 29, 2020.

narration.text: America's train safety system arrived 5 years late.
Congress set a 2015 deadline. It finished in 2020.
The system can override a crew and stop a train.
By June 2015, only 29 percent of APTA commuter systems expected to comply.
Congress extended the deadline to December 31, 2018.
Only 4 railroads made it. 37 more needed extensions.
It reached 100% of required track on December 29, 2020.
That's why rail safety tech is a coordination problem, not a gadget.

records.topic: The 1,450 °C Kiln Behind Every Road and Bridge
records.coreQuestion: Why are cement kilns so hard to decarbonise, even with clean fuel?
records.openingLine: Every bridge starts in a 1,450 °C kiln.
records.secondBeat: Cement kilns emit about 2.5% of human-made carbon.
records.dependency: Concrete for roads, bridges and buildings depends on clinker made in cement kilns.
records.mechanism: Limestone and clay are heated until calcium carbonate releases CO2 and minerals partly melt into clinker.
records.bottleneck: Part of the emissions comes from the rock chemistry itself, not the fuel.
records.failureConsequence: A kiln outage cuts regional cement supply, delaying construction.
records.resilience: Imports of cement and clinker, and alternative binders, cover part of demand.
records.expectedConsequence: construction schedules slip when regional clinker supply drops
editorialTitles: The Furnace Behind Every Bridge
Why Cement's Emissions Are So Hard to Cut

facts.claim: Emissions from cement kilns are a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, accounting for around 2.5% of non-natural carbon emissions worldwide.
The emissions come from two sources: the fuel and the waste CO2 created from heating the silicate rocks.
900 to 1050 °C – the remaining calcium carbonate decomposes to calcium oxide (CaO) and CO2.
Typically, a peak temperature of 1400–1450 °C is required to complete the reaction.
The hot clinker next falls into a cooler which recovers most of its heat, and cools the clinker to around 100 °C.

narration.text: Every bridge starts in a 1,450 °C kiln.
Cement kilns emit about 2.5% of human-made carbon.
Limestone releases CO2 as it breaks down near 900 °C.
So even clean fuel can't remove all the emissions.
At 1,400 to 1,450 °C, the minerals partly melt into clinker.
A cooler then brings clinker down to around 100 °C.
Stop the kiln, and concrete supply for whole regions stalls.
That's why the hardest emissions to cut are chemical, not fuel.

records.topic: The Arctic Vault Backing Up the World's Crops
records.coreQuestion: What happens to a country's crop varieties when its own seed bank is lost?
records.openingLine: Why 4.5 million seed samples need a mountain.
records.secondBeat: Svalbard's vault lies 130 metres inside sandstone.
records.dependency: Plant breeders and national genebanks depend on duplicate seed collections as a last backup.
records.mechanism: Seeds are dried, sealed and stored at −18 °C inside permafrost rock to keep them viable for decades.
records.bottleneck: A single backup site holds duplicates for much of the world's crop diversity.
records.failureConsequence: If a national collection is destroyed and has no duplicate, those varieties can be lost for good.
records.resilience: Depositors can withdraw their duplicates to rebuild collections.
records.expectedConsequence: breeders lose traits they may need for future climates
visualScenes: entrance of the Svalbard vault in snow
editorialTitles: The Arctic Vault Backing Up Our Crops
Why the World's Seeds Sleep in a Mountain

facts.claim: The seed bank is 130 m (430 ft) inside a sandstone mountain on Spitsbergen Island, and employs robust security systems.
The facility has a storage capacity of 4.5 million seed samples.
Locally mined coal provides power for refrigeration units that further cool the seeds to the internationally recommended standard of −18 °C (−0.4 °F).
It being 130 m (430 ft) above sea level will keep the site dry even if the ice caps melt.
In 2015, researchers started sending seeds from the Middle East for safeguarding in Svalbard due to ongoing conflicts.

narration.text: Why 4.5 million seed samples need a mountain.
Svalbard's vault lies 130 metres inside sandstone.
It sits on Spitsbergen, deep in the Arctic.
Local coal power keeps them at minus 18 °C.
Sitting 130 metres above sea level, it stays dry if ice melts.
Since 2015, conflict has pushed Middle Eastern seeds into safekeeping here.
If a national genebank is lost, this is the fallback.
That's why crop diversity depends on one cold room in the Arctic.

records.topic: The Canadian Mineral Feeding the World's Crops
records.coreQuestion: Why does global farming depend on potash mined in so few places?
records.openingLine: Why farms need 71.9 million tonnes of potash.
records.secondBeat: Canada is the largest producer of potash fertiliser.
records.dependency: Crop yields depend on potassium fertiliser, most of it mined and processed as potash.
records.mechanism: Buried potash deposits are mined, refined into fertiliser and shipped by rail and sea to farms worldwide.
records.bottleneck: Potassium cannot be synthesised from air like nitrogen fertiliser; it must be mined from rare deposits.
records.failureConsequence: Sanctions, strikes or rail outages at major producers tighten fertiliser supply.
records.resilience: Farmers can draw down soil potassium for a season, at a yield cost later.
records.expectedConsequence: fertiliser prices rise before yields fall
visualScenes: crop field comparison with and without potassium
editorialTitles: The Mineral Behind the World's Harvests
Why Potash Can't Be Made, Only Mined

facts.claim: In 2021, the worldwide production of potash exceeded 71.9 million tonnes (~45.4 million tonnes K2O equivalent), and Canada is the largest producer of potash as fertilizer.
In 1943, potash was discovered in Saskatchewan, Canada, during oil drilling.
In 1958, the Potash Company of America became the first potash producer in Canada with the commissioning of an underground potash mine at Patience Lake.
By 1811, 70% of the total 19.6 million lbs of potash imports to Britain came from Canada.

narration.text: Why farms need 71.9 million tonnes of potash.
Canada is the largest producer of potash fertiliser.
That was the world's output in 2021.
Saskatchewan's deposits were found in 1943, during oil drilling.
Canada's first mine opened at Patience Lake in 1958.
Potassium can't be pulled from air like nitrogen. It must be mined.
Sanctions or rail strikes can squeeze farm supply fast.
That's why a few mines shape the price of food.

records.topic: The Salt-Splitting Plant Behind Clean Water
records.coreQuestion: Why do clean water, PVC and paper all depend on splitting salt with electricity?
records.openingLine: Clean water depends on splitting salt with electricity.
records.secondBeat: The chlor-alkali process makes chlorine and caustic soda.
records.dependency: Water treatment, PVC, paper and many chemicals depend on chlorine and caustic soda from chlor-alkali plants.
records.mechanism: Electrolysis splits brine into chlorine, sodium hydroxide and hydrogen.
records.bottleneck: The process is power-hungry, and chlorine is hazardous to transport, so plants sit near users.
records.failureConsequence: An outage can hit water treatment and plastics production at the same time.
records.resilience: Stored chemicals and supply from other plants cover short outages.
records.expectedConsequence: water utilities and plastics makers compete for the same chemicals
editorialTitles: The Salt-Splitting Plant Behind Clean Water
Why Chlorine Plants Are So Hard to Replace

facts.claim: 35 million tons of chlorine were prepared by this process in 1987.
In 2022, this had increased to about 97 million tonnes.
The process has a high energy consumption, for example around 2,500 kWh (9,000 MJ) of electricity per tonne of sodium hydroxide produced.
The caustic soda must usually be concentrated to 50% and the salt removed.

narration.text: Clean water depends on splitting salt with electricity.
The chlor-alkali process makes chlorine and caustic soda.
Chlorine output reached about 97 million tonnes in 2022.
In 1987, it was 35 million tons.
Each tonne of caustic soda uses around 2,500 kilowatt-hours.
Chlorine is hard to ship, so plants sit near their customers.
A plant outage can hit water treatment and plastics at once.
That's why one electrolysis step sits under so many industries.

records.topic: Why China Makes 76% of Rare-Earth Magnets
records.coreQuestion: Why does one country make three-quarters of the world's strongest magnets?
records.openingLine: Why 76% of rare-earth magnets come from China.
records.secondBeat: Neodymium magnets are the strongest permanent magnets sold.
records.dependency: Electric motors, generators and electronics depend on neodymium-iron-boron magnets.
records.mechanism: Rare-earth oxides are refined, alloyed with iron and boron, then sintered and magnetised.
records.bottleneck: Refining and magnet making are concentrated in China, with small output elsewhere.
records.failureConsequence: Export restrictions would stall motor and electronics production outside China.
records.resilience: New magnet plants in Japan, Vietnam and elsewhere add capacity slowly.
records.expectedConsequence: motor makers face longer lead times and higher prices
editorialTitles: The Magnet Supply Chain China Controls
Why Rare-Earth Magnets Are a Chokepoint

facts.claim: Developed independently in 1984 by General Motors and Sumitomo Special Metals, neodymium magnets are the strongest type of permanent magnet available commercially.
This magnetic energy value is about 18 times greater than ordinary ferrite magnets by volume and 12 times by mass.
As the temperature rises above 100 °C (212 °F), the coercivity decreases drastically until the Curie temperature (around 320 °C or 608 °F).
China produces more than 95% of rare earth elements and produces about 76% of the world's total rare-earth magnets.
Japan is the second-largest producer with about 7% of the global market.

narration.text: Why 76% of rare-earth magnets come from China.
Neodymium magnets are the strongest permanent magnets sold.
By volume, they store about 18 times a ferrite magnet's energy.
Above 100 °C, their resistance to demagnetising drops drastically.
China also produces more than 95% of rare earth elements.
Japan, the next producer, holds about 7%.
Export limits on magnets would stall motor factories worldwide.
That's why a small magnet is a big strategic chokepoint.

records.topic: The 27 Extra Seconds Added to World Time
records.coreQuestion: Why has the world's official time had to add 27 extra seconds?
records.openingLine: Why clocks worldwide have added 27 hidden seconds.
records.secondBeat: Since 1972, leap seconds have kept UTC near Earth's rotation.
records.dependency: Networks, satellites, markets and power grids depend on a shared UTC timescale.
records.mechanism: When Earth's rotation drifts from atomic time, a leap second is inserted into UTC.
records.bottleneck: Every system must apply the same extra second at the same instant.
records.failureConsequence: Systems that handle the leap second differently can disagree on the time.
records.resilience: Some operators smear the extra second over hours to avoid a jump.
records.expectedConsequence: mismatched clocks cause errors in time-sensitive systems
visualScenes: atomic clock versus Earth rotation diagram
editorialTitles: The Extra Seconds Hidden in World Time
Why Earth's Spin Forces Clocks to Pause

facts.claim: The leap second was introduced in 1972 (at that time UTC already lagged behind TAI by 10 seconds).
Since then, 27 leap seconds have been added to UTC, with the most recent occurring on 31 December 2016; thus the difference between UTC and TAI is now 37 seconds.
Glacial rebound shortens the solar day by 0.6 ms/century and the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake is thought to have shortened it by 2.68 microseconds.
Earth was spinning faster in 2020 and experienced the 28 shortest days since 1960, each of which lasted less than 86399.999 seconds.

narration.text: Why clocks worldwide have added 27 hidden seconds.
Since 1972, leap seconds have kept UTC near Earth's rotation.
The most recent was added on 31 December 2016.
UTC now runs 37 seconds behind atomic time, TAI.
Earth's spin varies. Glacial rebound shortens the day 0.6 milliseconds per century.
In 2020, Earth logged its 28 shortest days since 1960.
Every clock network must insert each extra second in sync.
That's why one second of drift is a global coordination job.
